lead: Propositional logic cannot say every student passes or someone forgot the ID. A predicate P(x) is a statement whose truth depends on a variable x. Replace x by a value from a chosen set, the universe of discourse, and P(x) becomes a proposition. Quantifiers let one statement speak about all values (∀) or at least one value (∃) in that universe. Program specifications, database queries, and mathematics use this language to state rules once and apply them to many objects.
prereq: You need 1.1 for propositions, connectives and truth tables, and 1.4 for valid arguments and modus ponens.

blocks.text: A predicate has places. P(x): x is even is a predicate. With x free, P(x) is not true or false until x gets a value. A variable is a symbol that stands for a member of the universe. The universe of discourse, also called the domain, is the set U of values allowed for the variable. For P(x): x is even, take U = {1,2,3,4}. P(2) is true and P(3) is false. If U = {2,4,6}, then P(x) is true for every x in U. A predicate can have more than one variable: R(x,y): x < y.

The universe changes truth. Let Q(x): x > 0. With U = {1,2,3}, ∀x Q(x) is true. With U = {-1,0,1}, the same formula is false because x = -1 gives Q(-1) false. Fix U before you judge any quantified statement. In exams, write U in words, such as all integers or all BTech students, before you write ∀ or ∃.

∀x P(x) is read for all x in U, P(x). It is true exactly when P(a) is true for every a in U. ∃x P(x) is read there exists x in U such that P(x). It is true when at least one a in U makes P(a) true. ∃!x P(x) adds exactly one: one a makes P(a) true and no other a does.

Let U = {1,2,3}. ∀x (x² ≥ 1) is true. ∃x (x + 2 = 5) is true, because x = 3 works. ∃!x (x² = 4) is true, because only x = 2 works in U. For a finite U, test every element for ∀; for ∃, stop at the first witness. The order of quantifiers matters when both appear: ∀x∃y R(x,y) is not the same as ∃y∀x R(x,y).

Negation swaps the quantifier and negates the body: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). So not every BTech student studies discrete mathematics means some BTech student does not study it. It does not mean every BTech student does not study it.

Quantifiers distribute over some connectives only: ∀x(P(x)∧Q(x)) ≡ ∀xP(x)∧∀xQ(x); ∃x(P(x)∨Q(x)) ≡ ∃xP(x)∨∃xQ(x). They do not distribute over ∨ for ∀ or over ∧ for ∃ in general. Binding: in ∀x P(x,y), x is bound and y is free. A formula with a free variable is not a proposition until that variable is assigned. The scope of a quantifier is the part it controls. Uniqueness negation: ¬∃!xP(x) means none or at least two, not ∃!x¬P(x).

Universal specification, also called universal instantiation, says: from ∀xP(x) infer P(c) for any named c in U. Existential specification is more delicate: from ∃xP(x) infer P(c) only for a fresh name c, not one already used.

Universal generalization says: if P(c) is proved for an arbitrary c in U with no special assumption, infer ∀xP(x). Existential generalization says: from P(c) for some c in U infer ∃xP(x). A quantified argument is valid when every universe and every interpretation that makes all premises true also makes the conclusion true. A single counterexample universe kills validity. The full proof templates and the CP rule appear in 1.7.

figure.caption: Ravi is inside the BTech set, which is inside the discrete-math set, which is inside the universe. The nesting shows why B(Ravi) and D(Ravi) are statements about one named member.

spec.aria: Three nested sets: the BTech set with Ravi sits inside the discrete-math set, which sits inside the universe.

examples.question: Universe is all students. B(x): x is a BTech student. D(x): x studies discrete mathematics. Given ∀x(B(x)→D(x)) and B(Ravi), prove D(Ravi).
steps: Apply universal specification with c = Ravi: B(Ravi)→D(Ravi).
Apply modus ponens to B(Ravi) and B(Ravi)→D(Ravi): D(Ravi).
Read D(Ravi): Ravi studies discrete mathematics.

traps: Changing the universe can change a quantified statement from true to false. Fix U first.
In ∀xP(x,y), y is free; the formula is not a proposition until y is assigned.
∀x(P(x)→Q(x)) with P(Ravi) gives Q(Ravi) by specification and modus ponens; it does not give P(Ravi).
¬∃!xP(x) means zero or at least two values satisfy P, not exactly one value satisfies ¬P.

quiz.a: The universe of discourse, or domain, is the set U of values that a variable in a predicate may take.

quiz.q: Why is P(x): x > 0 not a proposition when x is free?
quiz.a: Its truth depends on x. Without a value or a quantifier, P(x) has no definite truth value.
∀x(x² ≥ 1) is true because 1², 2², 3² are all at least 1. ∃!x(x² = 4) is true because only x = 2 gives x² = 4 in U.
From ∀xP(x), infer P(c) for any named c in the universe.

quiz.q: From ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)) and P(a), what follows by specification and modus ponens?
quiz.a: Specification gives P(a)→Q(a). Modus ponens with P(a) gives Q(a).

quiz.q: Is ∀x(P(x)∨Q(x)) equivalent to ∀xP(x)∨∀xQ(x)? Give a counterexample.
quiz.a: No. Take U = {1,2}. Let P(1) true, P(2) false, Q(1) false, Q(2) true. Then ∀x(P(x)∨Q(x)) is true, but ∀xP(x) is false and ∀xQ(x) is false, so the right side is false.

beyond: Not for the exam. Predicate logic is the input language of SMT solvers such as Z3, which check program assertions and hardware designs. SQL's EXISTS and NOT EXISTS are quantifiers over rows, and query optimisers rewrite them using the same negation laws. Prolog and Datalog treat predicates as programs. Formal verification tools for transport and payment systems use quantified invariants. Search next: SMT quantifiers, SQL EXISTS, Datalog semantics.
